transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-30 15:00 UTC | Duration 46m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Kim (Novus PM), Marcus Lee (Novus Eng), Leah Ortiz (Novus CISO)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick agenda: we want to walk through structured output / function calling in JSON mode, show how Console and Optimize recommend schemas and guardrails, and then talk pilot + security. Sound good?
[00:12] Jordan Kim: Yep, sounds great. We're particularly interested in generating structured product recommendations that can be safely executed by our storefront microservices.
[00:18] Marcus Lee: And latency is huge for us, we have 99th pct requirements around 180 ms for single-turn recs. Also curious about dedicated vs hosted.
[00:25] Priya Patel: Great context. I'll share my screen - apologies if the deck loads slowly. We'll start with a quick JSON mode demo, then show the Console where you can declare schemas and failure policies.
[00:38] Priya Patel: (demo) So here in the API you can set mode: "json" and pass a schema. Redwood will attempt to return strictly valid JSON matching that schema. If it can't, our structured-output guardrail will either 1) retry with a higher temperature clamp, 2) return an error payload, or 3) call a fallback function based on route policy.
[01:05] Marcus Lee: Is that strict validation on the service side or client side? We want to prevent bad payloads hitting our microservices.
[01:12] Priya Patel: Good question. Validation is server-side before we return the response, and you can enable an additional validation webhook that will reject any non-conforming payloads before execution. So yes, blocking is supported.
[01:23] Leah Ortiz: And is the webhook hosted by Redwood or do we host it in our VPC? For security we need control over sensitive PII checks.
[01:31] Alex Chen: You can do either. For Private deployments we offer a customer-hosted validation hook in your VPC. For hosted API customers you can use the Redwood-managed webhook or provide your own endpoint. We'll include details in the security pack.
[01:44] Jordan Kim: Show us an example schema please.
[01:46] Priya Patel: Sure. (typing) Example: we declare an object with fields: product_id (string), price_cents (integer), availability (enum), and actions array. Then we map function signatures to the actions items so the model can "call" the add_to_cart function using a strict payload.
[02:10] Priya Patel: Note — sometimes the transcription and auto formatting do weird things, like the console will show K V cache as K V, but the actual runtime supports kv-cache for prefix caching. Small UI quirk.
[02:20] Marcus Lee: How do you handle hallucinations where the model returns a product_id that doesn't exist?
[02:24] Priya Patel: Two layers: first, the schema can include an enum or restricted set; second, you can add a post-validation hook that cross-checks against your DB and either corrects or rejects. Redwood Optimize can suggest caching and schema tightenings based on observed mismatch rates.
[02:40] Jordan Kim: Can we see the function-calling flow end-to-end?
[02:43] Priya Patel: Yep. (demo continues) We invoke the API, model decides to call a function named get_inventory, it emits the args as JSON, Redwood captures that and maps to your configured endpoint. We show trace logs in Console with token-level latency and cost.
[03:05] Alex Chen: Important to mention: we support streaming structured outputs as well. If you want low tail latency, you can stream partial JSON fragments and have your client assemble and validate incrementally. That reduces 99th pct significantly in our tests.
[03:19] Marcus Lee: Streaming sounds useful. Does streaming increase the chance of partial or invalid JSON that could break our parser?
[03:25] Priya Patel: We provide a streaming-safe framing layer. The Console also has a streaming-to-json helper that reassembles and validates fragments. If reassembly fails, policy decides whether to abort or call fallback.
[03:36] Leah Ortiz: Encryption/keys question: where are outputs stored and who has access? We need KMS integration and audit logs.
[03:44] Alex Chen: We integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSMs for Private deployments. For hosted, customer-managed CMKs are supported for data at rest; audit logs with per-token metadata are available in Console and can be exported to your SIEM. We'll attach SOC2/ISO artifacts in the security docs.
[04:00] Jordan Kim: What about cost? If we lock down schema strictly we'll need more generation attempts maybe. How does that affect token cost?
[04:08] Priya Patel: Good callout — stricter guardrails can increase retries in some edge cases. Optimize provides suggestions like selective prefix caching and using quantized model variants for non-critical routes. In our internal benchmarks we saw up to 35% cost reduction with KV caching + right quantization without impacting semantic correctness.
[04:28] Marcus Lee: You mentioned dedicated. For our workload (peak 1200 qps but bursty) what's the recommended config?
[04:36] Alex Chen: For that pattern we usually propose a Dedicated pool with a baseline commit sized for expected sustained throughput and burst capacity enabled. We'll size initial pool in the SOW; Priya can run a small benchmark to estimate tokens/sec and expected concurrency.
[04:48] Priya Patel: I'll sketch a test: we run 1k concurrent short recs (50-80 tokens) and another with long context (1k tokens) to measure KV cache hit impact. We'll provide a sizing spreadsheet after the run.
[05:00] Jordan Kim: On the Console demo, can you show how rules and rollout work? We might want canary a schema change to 5% of traffic.
[05:07] Priya Patel: Sure. (demo) Here you can create a route, attach a schema, and create a rollout policy. Canary percent, automatic rollback on schema errors or increased latency — you can also route by region or customer tier.
[05:22] Marcus Lee: If a canary fails and we rollback, is there a graceful degrade? We can't have 500s to storefront.
[05:27] Alex Chen: Yes, define fallback rules: switch to a lighter model variant, return a cached response, or call an internal safe endpoint. Redwood supports automatic fallback chains.
[05:36] Jordan Kim: Ok good. How about observability — what do we get in the Console?
[05:40] Priya Patel: Token-level cost, per-route latency distribution, schema violation counts, function-calling success rates, and sample traces. You can export logs to S3 or SIEM.
[05:50] Leah Ortiz: On compliance we need export controls and residency. Can you host in our EU region only?
[05:56] Alex Chen: Yes, for Dedicated and Private you can pin region and deploy in EU-only zones. Hosted region isolation is available for higher tiers; we'll call that out in the SOW.
[06:07] Jordan Kim: Earlier you mentioned guardrails for third-party tool calls. We plan to have the model call a payments service for price checks — how do you prevent it from leaking tokens or secrets?
[06:18] Priya Patel: Redwood supports function signatures where secrets are never exposed to the model. We do the mapping server-side. For sensitive calls you can require an allowlist and you can mask or redact args in traces. Also, we support request-time tokenization and redaction policies.
[06:33] Marcus Lee: Any limitations on schema expressiveness? We have nested arrays and polymorphic actions.
[06:38] Priya Patel: The schema is JSON Schema-inspired. We support nested objects and arrays, and union-types via a discriminator field. For very complex polymorphism we recommend adding a small canonicalization function post-validate which Redwood can host in your VPC to transform into internal formats.
[06:52] Jordan Kim: Can you show a failure case?
[06:54] Priya Patel: Sure. (demo shows a forced schema violation) The model produced an extra field. Console shows the validation error, and because the route policy is set to 'block-and-log' it did not call the downstream function. It raised an alert and created a ticket in the integrated ticketing system.
[07:10] Jordan Kim: Nice. That aligns with our safety requirements.
[07:14] Marcus Lee: For the pilot, can we run with a small dedicated pool but keep data path inside our VPC?
[07:20] Alex Chen: Yes — we offer a private control plane with inference in your VPC for pilots. It requires some infra work but we've done quick on-prem or VPC pilots in 2-4 weeks typically.
[07:31] Leah Ortiz: What about pen tests and vulnerability disclosure?
[07:34] Alex Chen: We have a public security program, third-party pentests annually, and we can run a targeted assessment for a Private deployment. We'll include our contact and SLA for incident response in the security docs.
[07:47] Jordan Kim: How do we start the pilot? What's the minimal data you need?
[07:51] Priya Patel: We need sample payloads, expected throughput, a schema spec (we can start with a draft), and an endpoint for function calls. Marcus, you can drop anonymized examples and we can iterate.
[08:02] Marcus Lee: I'll anonymize product IDs and share a small set today.
[08:06] Alex Chen: Great. Next steps recap: Alex will send SOW + pricing + security pack. Priya will run the benchmark and share sizing. Marcus will provide sample data and a staging endpoint. Leah will send any compliance questions.
[08:18] Jordan Kim: One more quick question — do you have rate limiting per-token vs per-request? We want to throttle heavy embedding jobs separately.
[08:25] Priya Patel: Both — you can configure quotas by route, token, and embedding units. Console lets you set per-team quotas as well.
[08:33] Jordan Kim: Thanks, that helps.
[08:36] Alex Chen: Cool. We'll follow up with links: deck: https://redwood-internal.s3/structured-output-demo.pdf, security pack: https://redwood-internal.s3/security-pack.pdf, and the pilot spreadsheet.
[08:48] Marcus Lee: One tiny nit — in past demos I've seen function-calling map break when the model emits single quotes instead of double quotes. Is that handled?
[08:56] Priya Patel: Our structured-output parser tolerates common quoting issues and will attempt to canonicalize. If canonicalization fails, that's a validation error and will follow route policy.
[09:06] Jordan Kim: Alright, that was super helpful. Let's get the SOW and schedule the kickoff week of 7/6.
[09:11] Alex Chen: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

(End of recording)
